entries.title: Hominin footprints in an ancient estuary
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated geological age of the footprint-bearing layer, projected onto the calendar axis as an approximate range.
entries.summary: A footprint surface records several people walking across estuarine mud on a landscape now on the Norfolk coast.
entries.detail: The ancient inland river system drained through this area. Sediments and their palaeomagnetic and fossil evidence support the broad age range assigned to the footprint horizon.
entries.uncertainty: The estimated age comes from the deposits. The footprints identify hominins, with species attribution unresolved. The coastal pin is approximate.

entries.title: Worked flint in river sediments
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded Pleistocene age assigned to the artefact-bearing deposits from stratigraphy and environmental evidence.
entries.summary: Sharp flakes and a flint core are evidence of human activity in a warm Pleistocene landscape.
entries.detail: The artefacts came from deposits containing fossils of plants and animals. Pakefield represents a different episode of activity from the older Happisburgh footprint horizon.
entries.uncertainty: The age is an estimate based on the deposits. The pin marks the coastal locality.

entries.title: Early human bones and tools at Boxgrove
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded age assigned to the deposits that preserve the oldest known British hominin bones.
entries.summary: A lower leg bone and two teeth accompany an archaeological record of activity near an ancient shoreline.
entries.detail: The teeth and the tibia came from different levels. Comparison with other European fossils helps frame questions about the people who used this landscape.
entries.uncertainty: Species-level attribution is debated. The location marks the general archaeological area.

entries.title: Fragments of an early human skull
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded age of the Thames terrace deposits that contained the skull fragments.
entries.summary: Three pieces of the same skull were recovered at different times in river-terrace deposits at Swanscombe.
entries.detail: The Thames terraces preserve evidence of changing environments and repeated activity by early humans.
entries.uncertainty: The age is assigned from the deposit sequence. Early Neanderthal affinities are a scientific interpretation.

entries.title: Early Neanderthal evidence in Wales
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded Middle Pleistocene age of the fossil and archaeological assemblage.
entries.summary: Teeth and stone artefacts recovered in the Elwy valley provide early evidence of human activity in what is now Wales.
entries.detail: Museum Wales places the Pontnewydd assemblage in the Middle Pleistocene. Later Welsh cave finds record separate episodes of occupation.
entries.uncertainty: The age is approximate. The pin identifies the wider cave area.

entries.title: Ochre burial at Paviland
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded calibrated radiocarbon age for the burial.
entries.summary: The remains of a young man were found with red ochre and worked objects in a cave above the Gower coast.
entries.detail: The name Red Lady of Paviland preserves the original excavator’s misidentification. The burial took place before the last glacial maximum, when the landscape below the cave was different.
entries.uncertainty: Radiocarbon dating gives an approximate age. Coastline and cave accessibility changed over time.

entries.title: A possible early Irish trace on reindeer bone
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate age reported for the reindeer bone. The human origin of the mark is a separately qualified inference.
entries.summary: A reindeer bone from the Castlepook cave assemblage has a mark interpreted by zooarchaeologist Ruth Carden as the result of stone-tool butchery.
entries.detail: If the interpretation and dating hold, the marked bone would place human activity in Ireland well before the dated bear bone from County Clare. The cave is also an important record of Ice Age fauna.
entries.uncertainty: This is a provisional attribution in a historic cave collection. The radiocarbon date concerns the bone and neither a settlement nor a continuous presence follows from it.

entries.title: Late Ice Age hunters at Cheddar Gorge
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded radiocarbon age of the sampled Late Glacial deposits.
entries.summary: Bones, stone tools and worked antler preserve evidence of activity as people returned to Britain late in the Ice Age.
entries.detail: Cut marks, broken bones and shaped skull fragments provide evidence of how people treated human remains. Animal remains also document hunting and butchery.
entries.uncertainty: The date describes sampled deposits. The duration and precise nature of the activities remain open to interpretation.

entries.title: Late Glacial stone tools in Scotland
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated typological bracket for the Late Glacial lithic evidence.
entries.summary: Flint points and other artefacts indicate activity by hunter-gatherers in southern Scotland towards the end of the last Ice Age.
entries.detail: The assemblage has technological parallels with late glacial hunters on the European mainland. Similarities help date artefacts recovered outside a secure primary layer.
entries.uncertainty: The span represents technological comparison. Field locations are generalized, and recovery from moved material limits precision.

entries.title: Late Ice Age remains at Kendrick’s Cave
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded radiocarbon age of the recovered human remains.
entries.summary: Human remains from the cave preserve a late-glacial funerary record and some of Britain’s earliest recovered human DNA.
entries.detail: The studied individual and the sample from Gough’s Cave have different ancestry affinities. Both belong to a small, regionally uneven set of surviving remains.
entries.uncertainty: Sample age and ancestry are evidence for individuals. The Llandudno pin marks the vicinity of the cave.

entries.title: A butchered bear bone in County Clare
entries.dateMeaning: Calibrated range of one radiocarbon determination from the cut-marked bone, measured before 1950.
entries.summary: Cut marks on a bear kneecap from the Alice and Gwendoline cave assemblage provide dated evidence of a late-glacial human presence in Ireland.
entries.detail: Microscopic study of the marks and radiocarbon assays link a human action to a datable animal bone.
entries.uncertainty: The cut bone dates an activity. Cave locality is approximate and a permanent settlement has not been demonstrated.

entries.title: Engravings at Creswell Crags
entries.dateMeaning: A minimum age for an engraving, inferred from dated flowstone that formed above it.
entries.summary: A dated layer of mineral growth over an engraving places people’s image-making in the Late Upper Palaeolithic.
entries.detail: The date constrains when the engraving could already have existed. The gorge preserves other traces of Late Ice Age human activity.
entries.uncertainty: The flowstone provides a minimum age. It does not record the year the figure was engraved.

entries.title: Work and shelter beside a postglacial lake
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded estimate for the changing complex of lakeside Mesolithic activity.
entries.summary: A Mesolithic site on a former lakeshore preserved timber, animal bone, tools and worked antler in waterlogged deposits.
entries.detail: Repeated visits and the preservation of normally fragile organic materials allow questions about seasonal life. Antler headdresses and traces of timber structures represent different activities in the landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The range gives a broad bracket around activity across the site. Individual features have their own dates.

entries.title: Early postglacial hearths near the Forth
entries.dateMeaning: Rounded calibration bracket for early Mesolithic activity.
entries.summary: Hearths, flint and charred hazelnut shells document visits to a landscape beside the River Almond and Firth of Forth.
entries.detail: Radiocarbon dating of organic material puts Cramond among Scotland’s early Mesolithic localities. The shoreline people knew lay in a landscape undergoing sea-level change.
entries.uncertainty: The range is an approximate bracket for the sampled activity. The pin marks the Cramond locality.

entries.title: Early Mesolithic activity by the Bann
entries.dateMeaning: Bayesian radiocarbon chronology for the initial period of Mesolithic activity.
entries.summary: Circular patterns of postholes and pits mark Mesolithic occupation above the River Bann.
entries.detail: Excavations found evidence of hunting, fishing and food processing. The distribution of pits and structures continues to be studied.
entries.uncertainty: Radiocarbon models and calibration affect the limits of the short early phase. The pin is approximate.

entries.title: Mesolithic cremation beside the Shannon
entries.dateMeaning: Calibrated radiocarbon range of the earliest cremation pit.
entries.summary: A pit contained cremated bone and a ground stone axe at a riverside Mesolithic burial site.
entries.detail: Microwear analysis helped reconstruct the axe’s short history before burial. The finds provide direct evidence about funerary practices among early hunter-gatherers in Ireland.
entries.uncertainty: The calibrated range applies to the early cremation, and the riverside pin is approximate.

entries.title: Storegga tsunami deposits in Shetland
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate age of the tsunami from dated sediments.
entries.summary: Sediment carried inland by a tsunami records the effects of a submarine slide off Norway.
entries.detail: Coastal deposits across the North Sea help reconstruct the local reach of this event and reveal interaction between sea level and topography.
entries.uncertainty: The date is rounded. Evidence for the wave establishes inundation at particular locations, with human impacts difficult to quantify.

entries.title: A pegged timber walkway through the Levels
entries.dateMeaning: Dendrochronological felling dates for wood used in the original trackway.
entries.summary: The Sweet Track crossed wet ground. Preserved timbers made precise tree-ring dating possible.
entries.detail: Boards and supports recorded a route through a landscape where movement depended on seasonal water and access to drier places.
entries.uncertainty: The dates refer to felling and construction evidence for a specific structure.

entries.title: Stone field walls beneath blanket bog
entries.dateMeaning: A broad bracket for early agricultural activity in the palaeoenvironmental model, rather than an independently measured date for every field wall.
entries.summary: Buried walls preserve a large system of enclosed land on the north Mayo coast.
entries.detail: The relationship between peat growth and the buried walls is central to understanding how open farmland became blanket bog. Nearby archaeological context includes houses and tombs.
entries.uncertainty: A Neolithic interpretation is supported by one environmental reconstruction. Other researchers date some field systems later. The interval has no site-wide certainty.

entries.title: Two early stone houses in Orkney
entries.dateMeaning: Broad reported calibration bracket for the sampled house sequence.
entries.summary: Two adjoining houses preserve partitions and furniture fixed in stone.
entries.detail: Pottery, animal remains and shells supplement the architecture with evidence of work, food and life near the coast. The sea has altered the original setting.
entries.uncertainty: The dates bracket a broad phase of Neolithic use. Specific architectural changes have a different level of dating precision.

entries.title: An early farming gathering place
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Intermittent ditches on the hill enclose a place used by Neolithic communities for gatherings and deposition.
entries.detail: Pottery and animal bone provide evidence of activity in and around a causewayed enclosure. It precedes the main Avebury stone circle.
entries.uncertainty: The range gives the approximate period of early enclosure activity. The purposes of different deposits are interpreted from archaeology.

entries.title: Passage tomb in Brú na Bóinne
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated date of the documented event or archaeological evidence.
entries.summary: A long passage and inner chamber sit within a mound whose entrance aligns towards the winter solstice sunrise.
entries.detail: Newgrange forms part of a wider archaeological landscape with Knowth and Dowth. The monuments preserve carved stones and evidence of communal funerary practices.
entries.uncertainty: The date gives the approximate main construction period. Use of the site extended beyond the original building phase.

entries.title: Neolithic houses joined by passages
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Stone furniture and hearths survive within partly sunken structures grouped near the Bay of Skaill.
entries.detail: Midden accumulated around the structures. The arrangement of buildings and passages changed during the settlement’s use.
entries.uncertainty: The interval covers multiple phases and building forms. The original shoreline setting differed from the present one.

entries.title: Passage tomb built inside an older enclosure
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated date of the documented event or archaeological evidence.
entries.summary: The monument preserves a sequence from a henge and stones to a passage tomb with a mound.
entries.detail: Light reaches into the chamber near the summer solstice. Excavated deposits and a carved stone record multiple ways of using the site.
entries.uncertainty: Approximate dating places the monument in the later Neolithic. Its individual phases and later activity span a wider period.

entries.title: Earthwork and tomb south of Belfast
entries.dateLabel: Later Neolithic, third millennium BCE bracket
entries.dateMeaning: Broad period attribution for the earthwork and tomb. The older timber enclosure nearby has separate excavation dates.
entries.summary: A large circular enclosure and the remains of a passage tomb survive in a landscape with other Neolithic funerary and ceremonial sites.
entries.detail: Finds around Ballynahatty show repeated modification and activity in the wider landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The Neolithic date is approximate and the relationship between structures is reconstructed from surviving earthworks and excavation.

entries.title: Standing stones and a later tomb on Lewis
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A stone circle and lines of uprights dominate a low ridge on the Isle of Lewis.
entries.detail: People later built a chambered cairn within the arrangement. Other nearby stone settings show that the monument belonged to a broader landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The range gives a broad construction bracket. Proposed astronomical functions remain subjects of interpretation.

entries.title: Deep shafts for high-quality flint
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Late Neolithic miners cut through chalk to reach seams of flint. Antler picks and discarded material survive underground.
entries.detail: The flint could be shaped into tools and moved through exchange networks. The shafts show skilled work and a large investment of labour.
entries.uncertainty: The interval covers the main late Neolithic mining phase. Later activity at the site had separate dates.

entries.title: Early mining and working of Irish copper
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Early Bronze Age finds and workings at Ross Island preserve evidence of copper production near the Lakes of Killarney.
entries.detail: The camps and workings contain mining debris. Metal from western Ireland circulated through networks beyond its places of extraction.
entries.uncertainty: The approximate dates refer to early mining activity. Metal-source attribution depends on archaeological and chemical analysis.

entries.title: Bronze Age copper workings on the Great Orme
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A network of tunnels preserves evidence of the extraction of copper ore in north Wales.
entries.detail: Mining involved following ore-bearing veins through limestone. Surface debris and underground workings help reconstruct where and how people worked.
entries.uncertainty: The span gives an approximate bracket for Bronze Age work. Output varies by phase and estimates differ.

entries.title: Stone circles and cairns under peat
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A cluster of low stone circles, rows and cairns was uncovered in a boggy landscape.
entries.detail: The group includes several forms and construction episodes. Peat helped preserve the arrangement and gives evidence of environmental change.
entries.uncertainty: The date bracket summarizes a broad Bronze Age context. Individual circles are less precisely dated.

entries.title: A sewn-plank boat at Dover
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated date of the documented event or archaeological evidence.
entries.summary: Preserved oak planks of a Bronze Age boat were found in waterlogged ground in Dover.
entries.detail: Woodworking and joining methods document an investment in moving people or goods across water. The surviving portion leaves questions about total size and voyages.
entries.uncertainty: The date is approximate. The pin marks the waterfront find area, rather than a reconstructed route.

entries.title: Late Bronze Age activity on the Aran Islands
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Excavation at the cliff-top fort identified settlement activity and Late Bronze Age deposits.
entries.detail: The surviving enclosure walls belong to a long sequence. Finds and construction evidence show how people used and modified the cliff edge over time.
entries.uncertainty: The date bracket covers an early phase. The standing defences developed across later phases.

entries.title: Houses, food and textiles at Must Farm
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A settlement built over a wet channel burned. The collapse preserved objects near where people last used them.
entries.detail: Surviving objects include textiles, wooden artefacts and vessels with food traces. This short-lived settlement gives an unusually detailed view of domestic work.
entries.uncertainty: The interval is the project’s archaeological dating bracket. Duration before the fire was much shorter.

entries.title: An Iron Age causeway and offerings by the Witham
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Large timbers formed a crossing in wet ground. Nearby excavations recovered metalwork and other deposits.
entries.detail: The waterlogged setting preserved organic details and helped date the structure. A crossing and deposition site could operate in the same landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The interval bounds selected Iron Age use. Individual timber phases are more precisely dated.

entries.title: An Iron Age settlement with roundhouses
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Excavation identified roundhouse sites within a fortified settlement.
entries.detail: Postholes and occupation traces explain the reconstructed dwellings. The reconstructions depend on archaeological evidence and experimental building.
entries.uncertainty: The range is a broad bracket for the Iron Age phase. Later use of the site extended into Roman times.

entries.title: Metalwork deposited in a watery place
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Weapons, tools and fittings from vehicles and harnesses survived around a former lake margin.
entries.detail: The objects were put into the water over time. Examples illuminate skilled metalworking and regional exchange as well as possible ritual deposition.
entries.uncertainty: The range dates multiple objects. A single explanation for all deposits remains uncertain.

entries.title: A tall double-walled broch
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Mousa preserves an Iron Age dry-stone tower with passages and stairs within its wall.
entries.detail: Its survival makes the building details unusually visible. Brochs belonged to settlements whose social and defensive uses varied.
entries.uncertainty: The construction bracket is approximate. Function and later phases are interpreted from material and written evidence.

entries.title: Gold neck ornament and miniature boat
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A hoard found near the mouth of the Roe included a decorated gold collar and a small boat with equipment.
entries.detail: The objects show the skill required to form thin gold and elaborate designs. The miniature boat evokes real transport and seafaring in Iron Age society.
entries.uncertainty: The mapped point represents the approximate find vicinity. The circumstances of deposition are debated.

entries.title: A large circular timber structure at Emain Macha
entries.dateMeaning: Dendrochronological date for the principal post of the best-known timber structure.
entries.summary: Tree-ring dating anchors a large timber structure within a complex with several successive building phases.
entries.detail: Excavations found that the circular structure was filled with stones and burned or incorporated into a mound. Geophysics has broadened the known extent of earlier structures.
entries.uncertainty: The year dates the central timber. The full sequence spans more time, and links to figures in later literature are interpretive.

entries.title: Landing defences at a Roman port
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Roman ditches and a gate mark a landing and supply point associated with the Claudian invasion.
entries.detail: The site later became a town and military installation. The former island and channel helped make it a useful port.
entries.uncertainty: The location is the known Richborough site. The ditch evidence supports a landing base while the full invasion route is debated.

entries.title: Watling Street connects early Roman towns
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A major road linked Dover and Canterbury to London, then passed through St Albans and Towcester towards Wroxeter.
entries.detail: Archaeology at places including Towcester links settlement development to the road. The infrastructure carried official, military and commercial movements.
entries.uncertainty: The dates bracket early construction and use. The mapped connection is schematic, with the surviving Kilsby segment documented separately.

entries.title: A legionary fortress at Isca
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Barracks, baths and an amphitheatre preserve part of a Roman legionary centre by the Usk.
entries.detail: The garrison depended on widespread systems of supply and labour. The surrounding civilian community formed another part of the settlement.
entries.uncertainty: The dates bracket early fortress construction. Later building and use lasted for centuries.

entries.title: Roman fort near the Menai Strait
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: The fort at Segontium formed part of Rome’s occupation of north Wales.
entries.detail: Buildings and inscriptions preserve evidence of a long garrison history. The adjacent strait helped give the locality strategic importance.
entries.uncertainty: The interval is the approximate establishment date. The remains include successive rebuilding phases.

entries.title: Dere Street links forts across the borderlands
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A Roman road entered what is now southeast Scotland and passed the fort near modern Melrose.
entries.detail: It formed part of a larger corridor between York and Roman military installations farther north. Later armies and travellers reused stretches of the road.
entries.uncertainty: The start date reflects archaeological dating to the first century. The connection to York is schematic.

entries.title: A Roman fort and crossing of the Tweed
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Military roads and a strategic river crossing shaped Roman activity at Trimontium.
entries.detail: Archaeological remains include fort phases and an extensive complex. Roman forces returned in later periods, and the surrounding communities had their own histories.
entries.uncertainty: The dates bracket an early phase. Occupation and rebuilding at the site were intermittent.

entries.title: From legionary base to civilian town
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A Roman town developed at the site of an earlier legionary fortress near the Severn.
entries.detail: Public buildings and domestic plots supported an urban community. The baths and market buildings belonged to a town whose urban fabric changed over time.
entries.uncertainty: The range covers early town development and major building works. Site activity extends beyond it.

entries.title: Building a Roman frontier across northern Britain
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: The wall, ditches, forts, roads and gates brought a new military infrastructure to the Tyne–Solway corridor.
entries.detail: Design and garrison arrangements changed during building. The frontier made some movement more controlled, while the road and gates provided connections.
entries.uncertainty: The interval gives a broad initial construction phase. The pin marks one sector of the much longer frontier.

entries.title: A turf frontier between the Forth and Clyde
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: The Roman army built a turf rampart, ditch, forts and a military road farther north than Hadrian’s Wall.
entries.detail: Forts and installations structured a line of communication and control. The Antonine frontier was occupied for a relatively short time before Rome returned to the southern line.
entries.uncertainty: The dates mark the beginning of construction. The pin is representative of a corridor approximately 60 kilometres long.

entries.title: Tara’s role in early Irish kingship
entries.dateMeaning: Broad time frame for early medieval royal associations.
entries.summary: An extensive monument landscape came to hold an important place in traditions of early Irish kingship.
entries.detail: Earthworks and a much older burial mound survive, while texts help reconstruct later ceremonies and political significance.
entries.uncertainty: The range represents selected early medieval royal associations. The roles and dates of specific structures vary.

entries.title: A Shannon crossing and monastic community
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A religious community associated with Ciarán developed by a junction of overland and river routes.
entries.detail: People later built churches, crosses and towers at the site. Burials and craft evidence document centuries of activity.
entries.uncertainty: The mid-sixth-century foundation date follows the historical tradition. Most surviving structures belong to later phases.

entries.title: Metalworking and kingship at Dunadd
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A fortified rocky hill became an important site within Dál Riata.
entries.detail: Small finds show craft production and access to imported goods. A carved footprint near the summit has been interpreted in connection with inauguration.
entries.uncertainty: The interval gives a bracket for major early medieval activity. The exact role of individual carvings is debated.

entries.title: Monastic settlement in a Wicklow valley
entries.dateLabel: Later sixth century CE, traditional foundation
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: The monastic community traditionally associated with Kevin occupied a valley framed by lakes and steep slopes.
entries.detail: The best-preserved stone structures, including a round tower, belong to later phases of a long-lived ecclesiastical site.
entries.uncertainty: The range gives the traditional era of the founder. No exact building year is assigned to the early community.

entries.title: Columba’s community on Iona
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated date of the documented event or archaeological evidence.
entries.summary: Columba and companions are traditionally recorded as founding a monastery on the island in 563.
entries.detail: The community took part in networks spanning Ireland and Britain. Carved crosses and early medieval sculpture survive alongside later abbey buildings.
entries.uncertainty: The foundation is a historical tradition supported by later accounts. The surviving abbey fabric largely postdates it.

entries.title: A ship burial and East Anglian power
entries.dateMeaning: Estimated date of the documented event or archaeological evidence.
entries.summary: A burial mound contained a ship imprint and a chamber with armour, vessels and other objects.
entries.detail: The finds connect elite households to craft and exchange networks across the North Sea and beyond. The material preserved in the burial reflects selective display.
entries.uncertainty: The burial is generally dated to the early seventh century. The identity of the person commemorated is uncertain.

entries.title: A tidal mill at an early Irish monastery
entries.dateMeaning: Tree-ring dating places the earliest tide mill at the start of the seventh century.
entries.summary: Water stored behind a dam drove a mill as the tide receded.
entries.detail: The excavation revealed early medieval engineering in the intertidal zone. Timbers and other remains helped reconstruct both the mill mechanism and changes to the shore.
entries.uncertainty: The dating refers to the earliest mill timbers. Successive mills had their own construction histories.

entries.title: Aidan’s monastery in Northumbria
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: A community founded by Aidan became a religious and artistic centre connected to Iona and the Northumbrian court.
entries.detail: Books, sculpture and records of holy people show the community’s reach. The tidal crossing shaped access to the island.
entries.uncertainty: The year follows the historical record of the foundation. The surviving priory buildings chiefly belong to the later refoundation.

entries.title: A Pictish monastery and its workshops
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Excavation near the Tarbat Old Parish Church uncovered workshops, carved stone and traces of an early medieval monastery.
entries.detail: Finds record specialised production as well as connections to ecclesiastical communities elsewhere. This eastern site complements evidence from Iona.
entries.uncertainty: Dating and function are archaeological reconstructions. The range covers a selected period of flourishing.

entries.title: Pictish remains and Norse buildings on Orkney
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: An island reached by tidal causeway preserves evidence of Pictish activity and a later Norse settlement.
entries.detail: The locality illustrates changing building forms and exchange connections at the edge of a farmed landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The dates bracket selected phases. The exact transition and relationship between communities are matters of research.

entries.title: An earthwork in the Welsh borderlands
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A broad bank and ditch crossed selected landscapes between Mercia and Welsh kingdoms.
entries.detail: The surviving sections vary in form and spread. At Chirk the line is visible in a borderland with many later layers of settlement and rule.
entries.uncertainty: The link to Offa rests partly on a later written account. Individual stretches and original functions remain debated.

entries.title: An illuminated Gospel book linked to Kells and Iona
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: The manuscript’s calligraphy and layered decoration preserve evidence of skilled early medieval bookmaking.
entries.detail: Columban communities in Iona and Kells shared networks of learning and religion. The manuscript was later kept at Kells and is now in Dublin.
entries.uncertainty: The production location is debated. The Kells pin marks its historical association, with links to Iona described in the source.

entries.title: A recorded raid on the island monastery
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: A seaborne attack on the monastery entered written accounts and provoked a response from the scholar Alcuin.
entries.detail: The raid became a well-known reference point in North Sea history. Ecclesiastical accounts preserve the shock experienced by the writers and their communities.
entries.uncertainty: The account is documented. The raiders’ exact origins, size and intentions remain uncertain.

entries.title: A Powys royal pedigree carved in stone
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A cross shaft associated with the rulers of Powys carried a lengthy Latin inscription commemorating named ancestors.
entries.detail: The text used memory and genealogy to make claims about power. A much earlier burial mound under the cross adds another layer to the site.
entries.uncertainty: Only part of the shaft survives and surface damage obscures the original inscription. Earlier copies inform readings.

entries.title: Norse houses added to a long-used site
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Longhouses and related structures preserve a record of Norse farming at Jarlshof.
entries.detail: People rebuilt the houses and outbuildings while bringing new material practices to a site with much earlier settlement phases.
entries.uncertainty: The interval covers successive Norse buildings. Neither site-wide continuity nor an exact arrival year can be inferred.

entries.title: A Viking base and emerging port at Dublin
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Written and archaeological evidence documents a ninth-century seaborne base and the later development of a trading town.
entries.detail: Wood, leather and metalwork from urban excavations preserve craft and exchange. A disruption in the early tenth century preceded a Scandinavian return in 917.
entries.uncertainty: The interval connects recorded events. The Wood Quay pin represents later urban archaeology and is not an exact location for the earliest ship base.

entries.title: Shops and households in Jórvík
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Timber buildings, tools and discarded goods from Coppergate preserve a record of craft production and trade.
entries.detail: Waterlogged site layers preserved wood, leather and organic traces. York’s inland routes extended to wider North Sea exchange networks.
entries.uncertainty: The dates bracket Viking-age urban deposits. The excavation exposed an area of the town with its own local sequence.

entries.title: A Norse port at Waterford
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: A site at a bend of the Suir developed as a seaborne stronghold and exchange centre.
entries.detail: Hiberno-Norse Waterford participated in Irish Sea and Atlantic networks. Reginald’s Tower marks the historic quarter, with surviving masonry from a later period.
entries.uncertainty: The year follows records cited by Heritage Ireland. The mapped tower is an orientation point for the early settlement area.

entries.title: Battle of Hastings and the Norman conquest
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: William of Normandy defeated Harold II’s army inland from the Sussex coast.
entries.detail: The victory opened the way to a new regime. Battle Abbey was later built near the recorded battlefield, where the layout of the fighting is still studied.
entries.uncertainty: The traditional battlefield area is mapped. Exact deployment and the place of Harold’s death are debated.

entries.title: A vast survey of land, people and resources
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Royal commissioners recorded estates, livestock, some inhabitants and values across much of England.
entries.detail: The resulting manuscripts help compare landholding before and after 1066 and reveal how the crown assessed resources. Survey coverage and detail differ by locality.
entries.uncertainty: The Winchester pin is a historical administrative reference. Surveying and writing took place through many districts.

entries.title: A round tower on a monastic island
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A tall stone round tower survives among churches, crosses and burial remains on an island in Lough Erne.
entries.detail: Movements along the lough connected the community with other settlements. Monastic activity is older than the surviving tower.
entries.uncertainty: The century bracket dates the standing tower. The island’s earliest ecclesiastical history comes partly from tradition.

entries.title: A Norse cathedral at Kirkwall
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Earl Rognvald began a cathedral dedicated to Magnus in the centre of Kirkwall.
entries.detail: The building shows Orkney’s links to Norse and wider ecclesiastical networks. Work and alteration continued after the foundation.
entries.uncertainty: The year refers to the foundation. The existing fabric combines several building campaigns.

entries.title: Ivory chess pieces on an Atlantic island
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Elaborately carved figures associated with Lewis belong to medieval networks carrying walrus ivory, objects and games.
entries.detail: Scandinavian workshops are one explanation for where the pieces were made. The cache connects the island to an exchange world larger than its place of discovery.
entries.uncertainty: The manufacture date is approximate. Original find circumstances and the precise Uig locality are disputed.

entries.title: An Anglo-Norman stronghold on the Boyne
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A major stone castle developed from the fortified seat associated with Hugh de Lacy.
entries.detail: The castle and crossing were part of a new system of territorial lordship. Its buildings and outer works changed over successive phases.
entries.uncertainty: The span covers selected early building activity. Later use and rebuilding extended beyond it.

entries.title: A castle on Belfast Lough
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: John de Courcy’s expansion into east Ulster brought a stronghold to a rock overlooking the lough.
entries.detail: The site gave access to ships and ways to supply and reinforce the garrison. Later builders enlarged the castle’s defences.
entries.uncertainty: The date refers to initial Anglo-Norman construction. Most visible parts have a longer building history.

entries.title: Construction of a medieval cathedral
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Work began on the cathedral associated with Bishop Peter de Leia at a much older sacred site.
entries.detail: Pilgrimage, liturgy and a rural ecclesiastical economy connected St Davids with travellers and institutions across the sea.
entries.uncertainty: The year marks the start of the surviving cathedral’s main campaign. Claims about the earliest religious community rely on earlier traditions.

entries.title: King John agrees to Magna Carta
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The charter addressed demands involving taxation, liberty and the relationship between royal and baronial authority.
entries.detail: It was soon annulled. Reissues in later years shaped its longer statutory and political history.
entries.uncertainty: The meeting area is mapped. The charter’s later constitutional standing developed after 1215.

entries.title: Knights and borough representatives summoned
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Simon de Montfort’s Parliament summoned county knights and representatives from some towns alongside prelates and magnates.
entries.detail: The meeting followed civil conflict within the ruling elite. The summons became an important episode in the history of parliamentary representation.
entries.uncertainty: Westminster marks the meeting place. Representation remained limited and power was unevenly distributed.

entries.title: An Edwardian castle and walled town
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Edward I’s conquest was followed by a castle and new walled settlement by the Menai Strait.
entries.detail: Access by sea helped supply the works. The fortified town and castle embodied military, political and economic changes following conquest.
entries.uncertainty: The beginning of the major campaign is securely recorded. The project developed in stages and some planned work remained incomplete.

entries.title: Robert Bruce defeats Edward II’s army
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The fighting near Stirling was a major turning point in the struggle over the Scottish crown and kingdom.
entries.detail: Control of routes and terrain mattered in the battle. The settlement surrounding the castle remained strategically important.
entries.uncertainty: The battlefield pin marks the general area. Landscape change and source interpretation affect the reconstruction of exact positions.

entries.title: A diplomatic letter asserting Scotland’s independence
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Named Scottish nobles addressed a letter to Pope John XXII defending Robert I and asserting their kingdom’s independence.
entries.detail: The document shows how political communities framed legitimacy through Latin diplomatic writing. Its surviving copy is itself a historical artefact.
entries.uncertainty: The letter is dated at Arbroath. It articulates contemporary political claims without mapping precise territorial control.

entries.title: Glyndŵr seeks support for an independent Welsh church
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The surviving Latin letter from Owain Glyndŵr to Charles VI of France set out demands concerning church governance and international allegiance.
entries.detail: The diplomacy forms part of a Welsh revolt in which military campaigns and claims to governmental authority developed across many places.
entries.uncertainty: Pennal is the place given in the letter. Political control shifted during the revolt, and the pin represents the correspondence.

entries.title: A stronghold of the O’Donnells
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A tower and castle complex by the River Eske preserves a centre associated with the O’Donnell lordship of Tír Chonaill.
entries.detail: Later occupation and rebuilding left additional architectural layers. The location was tied to routes between the bay and inland communities.
entries.uncertainty: The date is approximate for the earlier castle fabric. Later structures reflect changing ownership and rule.

entries.title: Orkney and Shetland pass to the Scottish Crown
entries.dateMeaning: Span of the documented events or historical process.
entries.summary: The islands were pledged in connection with a royal marriage and incorporated into the Scottish Crown.
entries.detail: Local governance and property rules carried earlier Norse features forward. Jurisdictional change and changes in speech and custom unfolded on different schedules.
entries.uncertainty: The historical dates concern the pledge and annexation. Kirkwall represents the islands’ principal medieval centre, and Shetland’s pledge followed Orkney’s.

entries.title: The Crown suppresses monastic houses
entries.dateMeaning: Span of the documented events or historical process.
entries.summary: Religious property passed to the Crown as Henry VIII’s government closed monastic houses across England and Wales.
entries.detail: The process generated inventories, surveys and disputes. At Fountains and elsewhere it changed estates, work and networks of welfare and devotion.
entries.uncertainty: The interval dates the wider suppression. The Fountains pin represents one house and its landscape.

entries.title: Tudor legislation remakes governance in Wales
entries.dateMeaning: Span of the documented events or historical process.
entries.summary: Tudor measures reorganised law, counties, courts and parliamentary representation in Wales and the Marches.
entries.detail: English became the official language of the relevant administration and courts. The legislation recast jurisdictions that had developed unevenly over centuries.
entries.uncertainty: The point is a representative Welsh administrative locality. The legislation was enacted at Westminster, and historical act titles use regnal dating.

entries.title: A MacDonnell stronghold facing the North Channel
entries.dateLabel: Later sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: The castle became a seat of the MacDonnells, whose relationships and political interests crossed the North Channel.
entries.detail: Archaeology and buildings preserve traces of the castle and a later settlement nearby. This coast faced networks in western Scotland as well as mainland Ireland.
entries.uncertainty: The interval covers selected MacDonnell phases. Some standing structures are earlier or date from different campaigns.

entries.title: The Reformation transforms church institutions
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: At St Andrews, Protestant reform and conflict transformed established religious houses during a broader change across Scotland.
entries.detail: Buildings and goods were stripped, damaged or reassigned. The changes combined local movements with politics within Scotland and across its borders.
entries.uncertainty: The interval marks the decisive public events and national settlement. Changes in worship and the built environment continued later.

entries.title: A complete Bible in Welsh
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: William Morgan’s Welsh translation of the Bible appeared in print in 1588.
entries.detail: Translation demanded choices about language that influenced later written Welsh. Its circulation was tied to institutions of worship and reading.
entries.uncertainty: The Welsh pin marks a parish closely associated with Morgan’s work. The book was printed in London.

entries.title: A university planted in Tudor Dublin
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Elizabeth I chartered Trinity College on the site of a former religious house outside the medieval core of Dublin.
entries.detail: The college embodied Tudor Protestant educational policy. Its relationship to the city and patterns of admission changed across later centuries.
entries.uncertainty: The founding charter fixes the date. The present campus includes mainly later fabric.

entries.title: James VI of Scotland inherits the English crown
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The Scottish king succeeded Elizabeth I, becoming James I in England and ruler of multiple kingdoms.
entries.detail: Distinct parliaments and bodies of law continued. The move of the royal court shifted connections between Edinburgh and London.
entries.uncertainty: Edinburgh marks James’s pre-existing royal seat. The change was a union of crowns, with parliamentary union occurring in 1707.

entries.title: Ulster leaders depart across the sea
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Hugh O’Neill, Rory O’Donnell, Cúchonnacht Maguire and followers embarked for continental Europe.
entries.detail: The contemporary participant Tadhg Ó Cianáin wrote an Irish account. The departure affected politics, landholding and government in Ulster in the years before planting new settlements.
entries.uncertainty: The first passage shown reaches the lower Seine port of Quillebeuf. The exiles’ later overland journey to Rome is a separate stage.

entries.title: A fortified plantation town by the Foyle
entries.dateMeaning: Span of the documented events or historical process.
entries.summary: A circuit of walls was built around the plantation city under the auspices of London companies.
entries.detail: The plantation redistributed land and encouraged new settlement in parts of Ulster. The walled town connected military requirements and commercial plans to a contested landscape.
entries.uncertainty: The dates cover the principal wall building phase. The displaced, surviving and incoming communities had different experiences across Ulster.

entries.title: A major engagement in the English Civil War
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Royalist and parliamentary forces fought at Edgehill in a conflict about political and military authority.
entries.detail: The war drew upon local resources and recruitment and was connected to struggles in Scotland and Ireland.
entries.uncertainty: The pin is approximate for the battlefield. A battle date records an event within a wider series of conflicts.

entries.title: Battle of the Boyne
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Forces of William III defeated the army of James II at crossings of the River Boyne.
entries.detail: The battle involved personnel and political interests from several European states. Military and political conflict in Ireland continued after the crossing.
entries.uncertainty: Calendar conventions affect the day given in historical accounts. The mapped pin marks the Oldbridge sector.

entries.title: Union makes the Kingdom of Great Britain
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Acts in Edinburgh and Westminster joined England and Scotland in a new parliamentary union.
entries.detail: The agreement established one Parliament of Great Britain. It preserved separate Scottish institutions including its legal system and established church.
entries.uncertainty: The date marks the union’s commencement. Edinburgh is one of two legislative centres tied to the event.

entries.title: Defeat of the Jacobite army at Culloden
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Government troops defeated the force led by Charles Edward Stuart on moorland near Inverness.
entries.detail: The defeat ended the 1745 rising and was followed by state repression and changes to aspects of Highland life. The armies combined people from varied backgrounds.
entries.uncertainty: The mapped point marks the battlefield vicinity. Culloden belongs to a wider conflict over the British and Irish crowns.

entries.title: A cast-iron bridge spans the Severn
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: A cast-iron arch was assembled above a river corridor already important for making and moving goods.
entries.detail: Work at nearby Coalbrookdale enabled the project. The bridge became a demonstration of what local ironworking could build at scale.
entries.uncertainty: The date refers to construction of the arch. The bridge formally opened later.

entries.title: Cotton mills and housing beside the Falls of Clyde
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Water power supported a mill settlement where workers lived close to the factory buildings.
entries.detail: David Dale established the mills. Later reforms associated with Robert Owen included schooling and collective services alongside disciplined factory labour.
entries.uncertainty: The range covers the start and selected early decades. The historical company and operation continued beyond them.

entries.title: The Liverpool slave ship Brookes and Kingston
entries.dateMeaning: Year catalogued for the specific transatlantic slave voyage.
entries.summary: The Brookes’s recorded 1787 voyage carried captive Africans to Kingston, Jamaica.
entries.detail: This venture linked Liverpool’s shipping and investment to forced transportation from the Gold Coast. An abolitionist diagram later made the ship an emblem of the trade.
entries.uncertainty: The Kingston point gives the recorded arrival port. A schematic association does not show the voyage’s African embarkation stop or exact ocean track.

entries.title: Ironworks open beside supplies of coal and ore
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Blaenavon’s furnaces and worker housing formed part of a rapid expansion of heavy industry.
entries.detail: Landscapes of extraction and transport tied the works to workers’ households, investors and distant buyers. The industrial town grew around these relationships.
entries.uncertainty: The year marks opening of the works. Mining, transport and housing changed for much longer.

entries.title: Government forces defeat insurgents near Enniscorthy
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Rebels in County Wexford established a camp on Vinegar Hill during the 1798 uprising.
entries.detail: Their defeat at the hill was part of a wider rebellion with distinct local leadership and political aims. Contemporary official accounts reflect the perspective of their creators.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks the hill and surviving windmill. Fighting took place across a wider area.

entries.title: The union of Great Britain and Ireland takes effect
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The acts of union replaced the separate Dublin Parliament with representation in the parliament at Westminster.
entries.detail: The new United Kingdom encompassed all of Ireland. Access to representation and office remained unequal and became a focus of further political argument.
entries.uncertainty: The date marks commencement. The principal Acts were passed in 1800.

entries.title: A steam locomotive hauls iron on a tramroad
entries.dateMeaning: Opening or documented demonstration of this rail link.
entries.summary: Richard Trevithick demonstrated his locomotive on an industrial route down the valley to Abercynon.
entries.detail: The tramroad moved goods towards the Glamorganshire Canal. The experiment showed that steam power could move a substantial load on rails designed in an era of horse haulage.
entries.uncertainty: The mapped line shows terminal association. It does not reconstruct every turn of the original tramroad.

entries.title: An iron aqueduct carries a canal over the Dee
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: A cast-iron trough took a navigable canal high above the Dee valley.
entries.detail: The aqueduct connected industrial districts with waterways. Stonework, iron casting and feeder water were all part of the engineering problem.
entries.uncertainty: The year marks completion of the aqueduct. The mapped point represents one crossing within a longer canal network.

entries.title: Parliament passes the Slave Trade Act
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The law prohibited British participation in the transatlantic slave trade following sustained resistance and abolition campaigns.
entries.detail: Slavery continued in British colonies. Subsequent measures had different dates, enforcement and exceptions, and compensation after the 1833 act went to enslavers.
entries.uncertainty: The pin locates Parliament. Effects depended on the roll-out of enforcement and the geographical reach of particular laws.

entries.title: Tenant households displaced from inland settlements
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Estate restructuring pushed farming households out of inland settlements in Sutherland.
entries.detail: Landowners made large areas available for sheep farming while many people were resettled on the coast or left. Evictions and new working arrangements changed where people could live and how they could support families.
entries.uncertainty: The dates cover selected Strathnaver clearances. Experiences, timing and causes varied elsewhere in the Highlands and islands.

entries.title: Cavalry attacks a reform meeting
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: A large reform meeting at St Peter’s Field called for parliamentary change. Armed forces entered the crowd and killed and injured participants.
entries.detail: Documents preserved by the National Archives reflect arguments about peaceful assembly, the authorities’ reaction and the treatment of those arrested.
entries.uncertainty: The field location is approximate in today’s street grid. Historical sources differ on the complete casualty count.

entries.title: The Stockton and Darlington Railway opens
entries.dateMeaning: Opening or documented demonstration of this rail link.
entries.summary: Locomotion No. 1 hauled an opening train from the Shildon area towards Darlington and Stockton.
entries.detail: The railway was built to carry coal and other traffic. It combined locomotive use with other forms of haulage as its service developed.
entries.uncertainty: The route link between Shildon and Stockton is schematic. Contemporary operations included several branches and different motive power.

entries.title: The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opens
entries.dateMeaning: Opening or documented demonstration of this rail link.
entries.summary: A public railway linked two industrial and commercial centres in northwest England.
entries.detail: It carried passengers and goods on a regular service using steam locomotives. Manchester’s Liverpool Road station preserves evidence of early terminal arrangements.
entries.uncertainty: Terminal markers express the documented connection. The map does not reconstruct track alignment through every intermediate site.

entries.title: The Merthyr Rising against debt and low wages
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Protests among industrial workers in Merthyr took place amid severe hardship and changed wage and employment conditions.
entries.detail: The response included soldiers and prosecutions. The episode is part of a history of politics and work in a town transformed by ironmaking.
entries.uncertainty: The point identifies the town centre. Crowd action and military engagements occurred at multiple sites.

entries.title: Ireland’s first passenger railway opens
entries.dateMeaning: Opening or documented demonstration of this rail link.
entries.summary: William Dargan helped build the line linking Dublin with the port then called Kingstown.
entries.detail: The coastal route connected an urban terminus with the developing harbour. Dargan went on to build many Irish railway lines and branches.
entries.uncertainty: The harbour pin marks the Kingstown end of the documented connection. The precise 1834 terminal arrangement differs from later stations.

entries.title: Chartists march into Newport
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Chartists descended from industrial districts to Newport, where soldiers fired on the crowd outside the Westgate.
entries.detail: The movement sought political representation through the People’s Charter. Participants and contemporaries disagreed over methods and intentions.
entries.uncertainty: The date and principal confrontation site are documented. The gathering involved multiple approaches and localities.

entries.title: Rural protests against tolls and hardship
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Protesters destroyed or attacked toll gates after disputes about charges and wider economic distress.
entries.detail: Some participants drew on a shared performance tradition around the figure called Rebecca. Resistance spread across west Wales without depending on a single place of assembly.
entries.uncertainty: The range covers selected years and Efailwen represents an early locality. Chronology varies by district.

entries.title: Six nineteenth-century counts of Dublin borough
entries.dateMeaning: Six historical census observations as tabulated for Dublin County Borough in the comparative 1926 report.
entries.summary: The Dublin borough total rose from 232,726 in 1841 to 258,369 in 1851, then varied across later census dates.
entries.detail: The separate 1891 Table V confirms the municipal borough count of 245,001. Dublin’s urban population extended beyond the scope of this borough series.
entries.uncertainty: This series follows the historical borough unit in the comparison table. Surrounding towns and newer administrative boundaries give different totals.

entries.title: Potato blight, hunger and relief during the Great Famine
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: Repeated crop failure in a society with unequal access to land and food produced widespread hunger, mortality and emigration.
entries.detail: Poor Law workhouses, soup kitchens and other relief measures left extensive records. Skibbereen became an especially visible example of distress, with local experiences varying greatly across the island.
entries.uncertainty: The date bracket follows the conventional broad period. The place pin represents one severely affected locality and the years differ by district.

entries.title: Famine-era departures on the Jeanie Johnston
entries.dateMeaning: Span of the documented events or historical process.
entries.place: Blennerville and Tralee Bay, County Kerry
entries.summary: The ship repeatedly carried emigrants from County Kerry to North America during and after the Great Famine.
entries.detail: Quebec was its principal destination, with other passages to ports in the United States. On eastbound voyages the vessel entered the timber trade.
entries.uncertainty: The connector shows a documented principal destination. It is schematic and excludes other voyages and routes.

entries.title: Linen factory buildings in north Belfast
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A mill complex developed near the waterfront as linen manufacturers expanded production.
entries.detail: Factory records and surviving ranges and machinery spaces give clues to the division of work and the demands of powering large-scale textile making.
entries.uncertainty: The bracket covers selected nineteenth-century construction. Later extensions and machinery changes had other dates.

entries.title: The Great Exhibition brings industrial goods to London
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Manufacturers, countries and colonial administrations sent goods and technologies to a temporary exhibition in Hyde Park.
entries.detail: The display combined industrial ambition, commerce and an unequal imperial order. Its collecting legacy helped build institutions that include the V&A.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks the original Crystal Palace site. The building was moved and re-erected in a different form at Sydenham.

entries.title: Harland and Wolff expands on Belfast’s waterfront
entries.dateMeaning: Approximate span of the selected historical or archaeological activity.
entries.summary: A nineteenth-century shipbuilding firm enlarged its operations on Queen’s Island.
entries.detail: Engineering work and ship construction drew on a broader urban economy in which linen already employed many workers. Belfast’s docks organised movement of people, goods and capital.
entries.uncertainty: The date marks the firm’s formation and the interval covers selected pre-1900 growth. The waterfront changed greatly after the recorded phases.

entries.title: London grows across four census checkpoints
entries.dateMeaning: Published retrospective census totals for the administrative county of London.
entries.summary: Four census checkpoints record growth from 2.81 million in 1861 to 4.23 million in 1891 within the historical comparison area.
entries.detail: The census used the administrative county as its comparison unit, including the City of London. Contemporaries also counted an outer ring using a separate definition.
entries.uncertainty: The consistent comparison area was tabulated retrospectively. It differs from the older registration county and from modern Greater London.

entries.title: A land act changes landlord–tenant relations
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: The Act established ways of setting fair rents and changed protections for qualifying tenants in Ireland.
entries.detail: Pressure over rents, eviction and ownership drove campaigning and legislation across Ireland. The statute also set out duties for a Land Commission.
entries.uncertainty: The map marks Dublin as an administrative reference. Westminster enacted the legislation and effects differed by locality and kind of holding.

entries.title: Crofters secure legal protections after rural protest
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.place: Braes, Isle of Skye, representative locality
entries.summary: The Crofters Holdings (Scotland) Act gave qualifying crofters stronger tenure protections and created a process for setting fair rents.
entries.detail: The law followed campaigns and conflicts over access to land in the Highlands and islands. Braes is one place associated with earlier resistance on Skye.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks a campaign locality. The act was adopted at Westminster and applied to defined Scottish crofting counties.

entries.title: Match workers strike in Bow
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Workers at the Bryant and May factory struck following complaints over pay and conditions.
entries.detail: The campaign drew public attention to women’s industrial organising. Worker testimony and reformers’ publications preserved different parts of its history.
entries.uncertainty: The pin marks the factory area. The dispute took place both inside the workplace and in public organising venues.

entries.title: The Forth Bridge opens to railway traffic
entries.dateMeaning: Opening or documented demonstration of this rail link.
entries.summary: A steel cantilever bridge linked the south and north sides of the Forth.
entries.detail: A fixed crossing transformed the rail network. Building the bridge demanded extensive labour and involved deaths and injuries among workers.
entries.uncertainty: The endpoints mark the bridge landings and the documented crossing between Queensferry communities.

entries.title: Census counts 255,950 people in Belfast
entries.dateMeaning: Population recorded on the date of the census.
entries.summary: The census returned 255,950 people for its City of Belfast tabulation.
entries.detail: The city’s manufacturing and waterfront helped concentrate an urban population. The record gives its own contemporary boundary and household classifications.
entries.uncertainty: The figure is the census city total. Modern definitions of Belfast and its surrounding settlements use different boundaries.

population.note: City total as tabulated by the census of Ireland.

entries.title: Census tabulation counts 128,915 people in Cardiff
entries.dateMeaning: Population recorded on the date of the census.
entries.summary: An official comparative census table records 128,915 inhabitants for Cardiff in 1891.
entries.detail: Growth drew on the town’s docks, administration and trade with coal-producing districts. The count records the scale of an industrial-era urban population.
entries.uncertainty: The source uses a county-borough comparison. Boundary conventions may differ from historical town or modern local-authority totals.

population.note: Cardiff county borough, as tabulated in the 1901 comparative report for 1891.

entries.title: Census counts 511,415 people in Glasgow burgh
entries.dateMeaning: Population recorded on the date of the census.
entries.summary: The Scottish census’s ages table reports a Glasgow burgh total of 511,415 people.
entries.detail: Much work in the city and Clyde valley relied on trade, industry and transport. The census classifies the inhabitants through a specific contemporary geographical unit.
entries.uncertainty: The figure is the census burgh total. The wider Clyde urban population and later enlarged city boundaries differ.

population.note: Glasgow burgh total in the 1891 ages table.

entries.title: The Penrhyn quarry strike begins
entries.dateMeaning: Date of the documented event.
entries.summary: Quarry workers struck in a dispute over working conditions, pay and control of labour.
entries.detail: Slate production connected northwest Wales to building markets around the world. The dispute made the pressures on quarry households visible in local businesses and networks of support.
entries.uncertainty: The entry marks the onset within the timeline’s 1900 limit. The dispute continued into 1903.
